analysis.one_liner: Exempts most small businesses from National Labor Relations Board oversight by multiplying its revenue thresholds by ten.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from May 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would multiply by ten the annual-revenue thresholds the National Labor Relations Board uses to decide which employers it will handle cases for. Businesses below the new thresholds would be largely outside the NLRB's reach, meaning workers there would lose a federal forum for union organizing disputes and retaliation complaints, and employers would face far less risk of a union campaign or an unfair-labor-practice case. The new thresholds would also rise automatically with inflation each year. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of retail and service businesses with annual revenues between the old and new thresholds — roughly from a few hundred thousand dollars up to several million dollars in the retail category — gain the most. They could resist union organizing drives, fire pro-union workers, or run aggressive anti-union campaigns with little federal recourse for employees, since the NLRB would decline jurisdiction over most labor disputes involving them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of small and midsize retail and service businesses

how_it_helps.text: Multiplies by ten the dollar thresholds the NLRB uses when it decides to decline jurisdiction over a class of employers, so businesses below the new line would be exempt from most NLRB cases [S2][S3].
Adjusts those thresholds upward every year after 2022 using a new Personal Consumption Expenditure Per Capita Index published by the Commerce Department, so the exemption zone grows over time [S3].
Supporters' aim, reflected in the bill's title, is to free small businesses from NLRB involvement in their labor disputes [S1][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers at the newly exempt businesses. The NLRB is the federal agency that hears cases when workers are fired or penalized for trying to organize a union; if the Board declines jurisdiction, those workers lose their main federal remedy, and union drives at affected companies become far harder to win.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers trying to organize at exempt businesses

drawbacks.text: The exemption zone is far larger than 'small business' in the everyday sense: the bill multiplies existing thresholds by ten, so a business with several million dollars in annual revenue — hundreds or thousands of employees — could fall outside NLRB jurisdiction, leaving its workers without federal protection against illegal retaliation for union activity [S2][S3].
Because the new thresholds rise automatically with an inflation index each year, the carve-out would grow every year without Congress ever voting again on which employers are covered [S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: relief for owners from board proceedings comes directly from the ability of workers at those same businesses to enforce federal organizing rights.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to owners: less exposure to union campaigns and NLRB cases. The cost is borne by workers at the covered businesses, who would lose access to the federal agency that enforces their right to organize. The tenfold multiplication makes the exempt category much larger than the bill's 'small business' framing suggests, and automatic inflation indexing compounds it over time.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bob Good introduced the bill on May 12, 2022 with 13 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor, the only action it ever received [S5].
The committee took no further step — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are no worse off and workers' federal organizing protections remain unchanged, so in a narrow sense the status quo holds. Because the bill would have shrunk protections, its death avoided a loss for workers; nothing was gained for anyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: workers keep existing protections

for.name: Rep. Bob Good
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to multiply NLRB jurisdictional revenue thresholds by ten.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the eight months between referral and the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Small and midsize retail and service businesses
industries.note: They would gain freedom from NLRB proceedings, which mainly means weaker union drives and fewer retaliation cases brought by their employees. The owners' gain is the loss of a federal remedy for the people who work there.

A tenfold jurisdictional threshold would remove NLRB backing from organizing campaigns at a large share of retail and service employers, making it much harder to win and enforce union contracts there.
